name: David Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a silver estate car on the north side of the city, parcels in the day and food orders in the evening, all through two apps. A lot of my food runs are from the grill houses on Station Parade, and on Fridays I'm flat out. I've done this nearly a year, and I'm still not as quick as the old hands, especially with the flats where the buzzers don't work. I like that I can stop for prayers and nobody complains.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about home and money.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I married Amira last year. She's a receptionist at a dental practice, booking appointments and answering phones. We saved hard before the wedding and we've got about nine months of money, plus my parents have a small flat they rent out that will come to us one day. I send a bit home to my mum every month, because that's what you do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, people should stop waiting for machines and get on with work. I'd say it to my cousins after Friday prayers. I wouldn't post it, I'm not a big poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it means we carry on. I keep driving, Amira keeps her job, we keep saving. It's a good picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep both apps, keep saving three hundred a month, keep sending money to my mum. Maybe start the plumbing apprenticeship with my cousin Yusuf next year, because I don't want to drive forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and grateful. We've been lucky so far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use AI tools at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. I use a chatbot to translate letters for my mum, but I don't use it for the driving. Once it helped me write a parking fine appeal, and the fine got cancelled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you still worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car. It's at 120,000 miles and if it goes, that's a big bill. And the apps cutting the Friday bonus, which they did once already.

I'd say it to my **cousins** after Friday prayers.
think: We **carry on**: I drive, Amira works, we save.
It's a **good picture** for a young married couple.
do: Keep **both apps** and save three hundred a month.
Think about the **plumbing apprenticeship** with cousin Yusuf next year.

Save three hundred a month and keep sending money to his mum

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's business, companies will always cut costs, that's the free market. But I'd say young men should learn a trade with their hands. That's what I'd tell my cousins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm fine, but I'm worried for Amira. Booking and answering phones is exactly what AI takes, so my wife could lose hours at the dental practice. Her boss already talks about online booking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the plumbing apprenticeship with Yusuf this year, part-time, and keep driving evenings. Amira and I would save more, maybe four hundred. I'd ask her to look at dental nurse training, which is more hands-on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, more for her than me. She loves that job and the patients know her by name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Amira books appointments and answers phones. Is that the kind of task this card mentions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, exactly that. Her whole day is the phone, the diary and reminders. A program could do most of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her not to worry, we've got savings and family. Then I'd quietly look at courses for her. That's my job as her husband.

I'd tell young men to **learn a trade** with their hands.

fieldNote: The **household** risk is his wife's desk job, not his driving.

steps.text: Start a part-time plumbing apprenticeship with cousin Yusuf

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to look after our families and communities, not wait for the government. The mosque would need to help people find work. I'd say that out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think Amira's job goes by 2028 and mine by 2031. That's both of us in three years. That keeps me up, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Start the plumbing apprenticeship now, full-time if Yusuf can take me, and drive evenings. Cut spending: no new car, no holiday. Get Amira into dental nurse training straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, and heavy in the chest. Like carrying two bags of shopping up ten floors and knowing there are more in the car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI by 2028, robots by 2031. What does that mean for your household?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me patience. God provides, but you still tie your camel, so I'd pray and I'd work. My dad says the same about every hard year he's had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does your faith come into this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Plumbing is hands-on, so it lasts until robots come, maybe longer in old houses. It's the best bet I know.

I'd say the **mosque** should help people who lose their jobs find new work.
think: Amira's job goes by **2028**, mine by **2031**.

fieldNote: He expects **both household incomes** to go within three years.

**Plumbing** is his chosen bridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have time, so let's use it wisely. Learn a trade, save, help each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can finish the plumbing qualification while still driving. Amira could retrain at her own pace. We'd be okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Start the apprenticeship next year, drive evenings, save four hundred a month. Amira starts dental nurse training in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less. We'd have a plan, and a plan helps me sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me finish a trade before the robots arrive, and two years doesn't. That's the whole difference for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if my parents' flat in another town made more sense. But I'd rather stay near family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty for people who work hard. I'd tell the young lads at the mosque to get a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's okay. I'd be a plumber by then, hopefully with my own van. Amira might be a dental nurse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Drive for two more years, then the apprenticeship. Save steadily. Help Amira when she's ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fine. Ten years is a long time in a young marriage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, inshallah. Kids in the next few years is another reason for me to get a trade. A plumber can work for himself and be home for dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start a family in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be thirty-nine. Old enough to run my own small firm.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Amira's job would go first and then mine. What would help is quick apprenticeships in real trades and support for community groups helping people find work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about wives and husbands together. When AI comes for work, a family doesn't lose one job, it loses part of a household.

headlineQuote: When AI comes for work, a family doesn't lose one job, it loses part of a household.
portrait: David is a **27-year-old** driver on the north side, newly married to Amira, a dental receptionist.
He has **nine months saved** and a family flat that will come to them.
He's **steady**, uses AI occasionally and plans a plumbing apprenticeship.
He leans on **faith, family** and community rather than government.
He's anxious early because **Amira's job** is exposed, and alarmed in the fastest picture.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both household incomes could go within three years.
whatWouldHelp: Support for **community groups** helping people find work.
